idiom_name: per-channel endpoint: decode message -> invoke service -> marshal result or route exception
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: attach one small endpoint per (input channel, service method) pair. The endpoint removes the envelope (payload plus the headers it needs, such as correlation id and return address), converts the payload into the service's argument types, invokes the service and marshals the return value into a reply message on the output channel, resolved from configuration or from the request's return address. Exceptions and unparsable payloads become messages on the error or invalid-message channel instead of being swallowed, and the acknowledgement is emitted only after the service (and its transaction) has completed. Keep the endpoint declarative and thin; the service stays ordinary code with no messaging dependency.
code_sketch:
on_message(channel, msg):
    args   = decode(msg.payload)                 # message -> service arguments
    result = service.invoke(args)                # ordinary call, no messaging types
    if result is not None:
        send(reply_channel(msg), encode(result))  # return address / output channel
    # on error: send(error_channel, describe(err)); do not acknowledge
    ack(msg)                                     # only after the service completed
pitfalls: Acknowledging on receipt instead of after the service completes turns a failure into silent message loss.
Sharing one mutable endpoint or service instance across concurrent invocations when the service was written for single-threaded use.
Leaving the reply contract implicit: a void or null return silently means no reply, and an exception nobody maps disappears.

Wrong move: passing the framework Message object straight into the service method to skip a mapping step -> the service signature now depends on the messaging API and the messaging-ignorant boundary is lost -> instead unpack the payload and the few needed headers into typed arguments at the endpoint (Spring Integration injects the payload or @Header values; NestJS hands the handler only the data payload).

Wrong move: catching service exceptions inside the handler and returning them as a normal error-payload reply -> the caller cannot distinguish failure from business result and a retryable failure never reaches an error path -> instead let the exception surface to the endpoint's error channel or error handler (Spring AMQP wraps it in ListenerExecutionFailedException for the container error handler; Azure Service Bus routes it to ProcessErrorAsync and leaves the message uncompleted) so it can be retried or dead-lettered.

Wrong move: trusting the auto-acknowledge default while the service performs non-idempotent writes -> Azure Service Bus AutoCompleteMessages completes the message as soon as the handler returns and Spring AMQP requeues every failure by default, so redelivery either double-applies the write or turns a poison message into an infinite redelivery loop -> instead acknowledge only after the service transaction commits, deduplicate by message id, and configure fatal-exception rejection (e.g. ConditionalRejectingErrorHandler) or a dead-letter path.
